newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress begins long road back.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress begins long road back.

text.p: Routed in general elections, India's Congress party has started to regroup by offering amnesty to rebels and pushing former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to the margins of the political battlefield.
Political analysts said the trend was towards party unity at the expense of Rao, who after being humiliated in polls that ended in May is now hobbled by three separate court cases.
Congress was not expected to pose an immediate challenge to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition.
But with the second largest number of seats in parliament, India's oldest party could flex its muscles once the unity drive is complete, analysts said.
"As of now I don't think there is anyone in the Congress party who could challenge Deve Gowda as prime minister," Pran Chopra of the Centre for Policy Research said.

"The most likely scenario is for the Congress party to eventually press a claim to share power with the United Front rather than displace the United Front," he said, referring to Deve Gowda's 13-party United Front minority government.

After an indecisive general election that threw up a badly hung parliament Congress and the United Front set aside their differences in May and forced the right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to relinquish power after only 12 days at the helm.
The BJP and its allies emerged as the biggest single party with 195 seats in the 545-member lower house. The disparate United Front has some 190 votes, while Congress controls 140.

To keep out the BJP, Congress, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence from Britain in 1947, agreed to back the United Front, which ranges from free traders to communists. But Congress did not join the government.

Congress and the United Front are united by the belief that the BJP's Hindu nationalist agenda discriminates against religious minorities, especially Moslems, and neither would want to face fresh elections right away.
Congress needs time to heal after the worst electoral showing in the party's history and to live down allegations of corruption.

Rao, who was thrust abruptly into power in 1991 after former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated during a general election campaign, stepped down as Congress party chief in September after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court to face charges of criminal conspiracy to cheat.
But he has refused to relinquish control over Congress's parliamentary delegation despite being named in two other criminal cases currently before local courts.
Pressure has steadily mounted on Rao to quit. On Friday, his interim successor at the head of Congress, Sitaram Kesri, summarily dismissed three Rao loyalists from senior posts.
"Sitaram Kesri is absolutely mad," newspapers quoted one of the embittered victims, B.P. Maurya, as saying.
Kesri chose the same day to readmit three Rao-baiters who had quit the party under the former prime minister. They joined Madhavrao Scindia, a keen rival of Rao who recently come back.
Newspapers said younger deputies, backed by the former chief minister of Maharashtra state, Sharad Pawar, were manoeuvring to force a fresh election for the Congress parliamentary leader.
Asked if Rao should step down, Kesri said it was up to him. "So far as I am concerned, I am running the organisation by excluding him from it, at least as long as he faces a crisis."
Chopra said: "I think Rao is practically finished off already in terms of challenging Kesri."
Elections to Congress leadership were not scheduled before February, giving Kesri and rivals time to plot. Only after that vote could Congress bid for a slice of power, Chopra said.
Deve Gowda on Sunday shrugged off the return of rebel Congressmen into that party's fold. "United Front is as strong as anything else," he said.
